Lymph_Anterior_Axillary_Nodes_Left.d: An anterior or pectoral group consists of four or five glands along the lower border of the Pectoralis minor, in relation with the lateral thoracic artery. Their afferents drain the skin and muscles of the anterior and lateral thoracic walls, and the central and lateral parts of the mamma; their efferents pass partly to the central and partly to the subclavicular groups of axillary glands.

Lymph_Anterior_Axillary_Nodes_Right.d: An anterior or pectoral group consists of four or five glands along the lower border of the Pectoralis minor, in relation with the lateral thoracic artery. Their afferents drain the skin and muscles of the anterior and lateral thoracic walls, and the central and lateral parts of the mamma; their efferents pass partly to the central and partly to the subclavicular groups of axillary glands.

Lymph_Apical_Axillary_Nodes_Left.d: An apical (or medial or subclavicular) group of six to twelve glands is situated partly posterior to the upper portion of the Pectoralis minor and partly above the upper border of this muscle. Its only direct territorial afferents are those that accompany the cephalic vein, and one that drains the upper peripheral part of the mamma. However, it receives the efferents of all the other axillary glands. The efferent vessels of the subclavicular group unite to form the subclavian trunk, which opens either directly into the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins or into the jugular lymphatic trunk; on the left side it may end in the thoracic duct. A few efferents from the...

Lymph_Apical_Axillary_Nodes_Right.d: An apical (or medial or subclavicular) group of six to twelve glands is situated partly posterior to the upper portion of the Pectoralis minor and partly above the upper border of this muscle. Its only direct territorial afferents are those that accompany the cephalic vein, and one that drains the upper peripheral part of the mamma. However, it receives the efferents of all the other axillary glands. The efferent vessels of the subclavicular group unite to form the subclavian trunk, which opens either directly into the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins or into the jugular lymphatic trunk; on the left side it may end in the thoracic duct. A few efferents from the...

Lymph_Appendicular_Nodes.d: The appendicular nodes are located along the appendicular artery. They can be missing.

Lymph_Brachiocephalic_Nodes.d: In front of the aortic arch and of its branches; along the brachiocephalic veins. They drain the thymus, the thyroid, the pericardium, the parasternal nodes. Evacuation: -left broncho-mediastinal lymphatic trunk -right broncho-mediastinal lymphatic trunk

Lymph_Bucinator_Node_Left.d: The bucinator lymph node or nodes are one or more lymph nodes placed on the Buccinator opposite the angle of the mouth.

Lymph_Bucinator_Node_Right.d: The bucinator lymph node or nodes are one or more lymph nodes placed on the Buccinator opposite the angle of the mouth.

Lymph_Central_Axillary_Nodes_Left.d: A central or intermediate group of three or four large glands is imbedded in the adipose tissue near the base of the axilla. Its afferent lymphatic vessels are the efferent vessels of all the preceding groups of axillary glands; its efferents pass to the subclavicular group.

Lymph_Central_Axillary_Nodes_Right.d: A central or intermediate group of three or four large glands is imbedded in the adipose tissue near the base of the axilla. Its afferent lymphatic vessels are the efferent vessels of all the preceding groups of axillary glands; its efferents pass to the subclavicular group.

Lymph_Central_Superior_Mesenteric_Nodes.d: Those of the superior mesenteric nodes located at the trunk of the superior mesenteric artery.

Lymph_Coeliac_Nodes.d: The coeliac nodes are located around the coeliac trunk and are the second filtration relay of the stomach, the duodenum, the liver, the gallbladder, the pancreas and the spleen. They efferent vessels form a part of the intestinal trunk, the others go directly to the chyle cistern.

Lymph_Cubital_Nodes_Left.d: One or two lymph nodes along the brachial artery inside the cubital fossa.

Lymph_Cubital_Nodes_Right.d: One or two lymph nodes along the brachial artery inside the cubital fossa.

Lymph_Cystic_Node.d: Big lympatic node next to the gallbladder.

Lymph_Ileocolic_Nodes.d: The ileocolic nodes are located along the ileocolic artery. Evacuation: Coeliac nodes

Lymph_Inferior_Diaphragmatic_Nodes.d: On the inferior surface of diaphragm, near the aortic hiatus.

Lymph_Inferior_Epigastric_Nodes_Left.d: Three or four lymph nodes along the inferior epigastric artery for its territory.

Lymph_Inferior_Epigastric_Nodes_Right.d: Three or four lymph nodes along the inferior epigastric artery for its territory.

Lymph_Inferior_Gluteal_Nodes_Left.d: They are located along the inferior gluteal nodes for the prostate and the proximal part of the ureter.

Lymph_Inferior_Gluteal_Nodes_Right.d: They are located along the inferior gluteal nodes for the prostate and the proximal part of the ureter.

Lymph_Inferior_Pancreatic_Nodes.d: On the inferior border of pancreas.

Lymph_Infraclavicular_Nodes_Left.d: One or two deltopectoral lymph nodes (or infraclavicular nodes) are found beside the cephalic vein, between the pectoralis major and deltoideus, immediately below the clavicle. They are situated in the course of the external collecting trunks of the arm.

Lymph_Infraclavicular_Nodes_Right.d: One or two deltopectoral lymph nodes (or infraclavicular nodes) are found beside the cephalic vein, between the pectoralis major and deltoideus, immediately below the clavicle. They are situated in the course of the external collecting trunks of the arm.

Lymph_Intercostal_Nodes_Left.d: The intercostal lymph nodes (intercostal glands) occupy the posterior parts of the intercostal spaces, in relation to the intercostal vessels. They receive the deep lymphatics from the postero-lateral aspect of the chest; some of these vessels are interrupted by small lateral intercostal glands. The efferents of the glands in the lower four or five spaces unite to form a trunk, which descends and opens either into the cisterna chyli or into the commencement of the thoracic duct. The efferents of the glands in the upper spaces of the left side end in the thoracic duct; those of the corresponding right spaces, in the right lymphatic duct.

Lymph_Intercostal_Nodes_Right.d: The intercostal lymph nodes (intercostal glands) occupy the posterior parts of the intercostal spaces, in relation to the intercostal vessels. They receive the deep lymphatics from the postero-lateral aspect of the chest; some of these vessels are interrupted by small lateral intercostal glands. The efferents of the glands in the lower four or five spaces unite to form a trunk, which descends and opens either into the cisterna chyli or into the commencement of the thoracic duct. The efferents of the glands in the upper spaces of the left side end in the thoracic duct; those of the corresponding right spaces, in the right lymphatic duct.

Lymph_Intermediate_Common_Iliac_Nodes.d: Those of the common iliac nodes located behind the vascular axis, between the medial common iliac nodes and the lateral common iliac nodes.

Lymph_Intermediate_External_Iliac_Nodes_.d: Group of external iliac nodes located behind the vascular axis, between the medial external iliac nodes and the lateral external iliac nodes.
Group of external iliac nodes located behind the vascular axis, between the medial external iliac nodes and the lateral external iliac nodes.

Lymph_Intermediate_Lumbar_Nodes.d: Between the aorta and the inferior vena cava. Around the inferior vena cava. Their first function is to be a second relay for the lymph nodes located more caudally. Secondly, they constitute a first relay for the draining of the suprarenal glands, kidneys, ureters, testis, ovaries, uterine tubes, uterine fundus and abdominal wall.

Lymph_Interpectoral_Nodes_Left.d: The small interpectoral lymph nodes are located between the pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles. They receive lymphatic fluid from the muscles and the mammary gland, and deliver lymphatic fluid to the axillary lymphatic plexus. These lymph nodes are susceptible to breast cancer, as the cancer sometimes spreads (metastasizes) to the interpectoral lymph nodes. It signifies retrograde spread of tumour.

Lymph_Interpectoral_Nodes_Right.d: The small interpectoral lymph nodes are located between the pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles. They receive lymphatic fluid from the muscles and the mammary gland, and deliver lymphatic fluid to the axillary lymphatic plexus. These lymph nodes are susceptible to breast cancer, as the cancer sometimes spreads (metastasizes) to the interpectoral lymph nodes. It signifies retrograde spread of tumour.

Lymph_Intrapulmonary_Nodes.d: The Intrapulmonary nodes or Lymphatic Vessels of the Lungs originate in two plexuses, a superficial and a deep. The superficial plexus is placed beneath the pulmonary pleura. The deep accompanies the branches of the pulmonary vessels and the ramifications of the bronchi. In the case of the larger bronchi the deep plexus consists of two networks—one, submucous, beneath the mucous membrane, and another, peribronchial, outside the walls of the bronchi. In the smaller bronchi there is but a single plexus, which extends as far as the bronchioles, but fails to reach the alveoli, in the walls of which there are no traces of lymphatic vessels. The superficial efferents turn around the borders of...

Lymph_Jugulodigastric_Node_Left.d: The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are large lymph nodes of the neck.

Lymph_Jugulodigastric_Node_Right.d: The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are large lymph nodes of the neck.

Lymph_Juxta_Intestinal_Mesenteric_Nodes.d: Those of the superior mesenteric nodes located very close to the small intestine.

Lymph_Juxta_Oesophageal_Nodes.d: They are located next to the oesophagus but belong to the lungs.

Lymph_Lateral_Aortic_Nodes.d: They are located on the left side of the abdominal aorta.

Lymph_Lateral_Axillary_Nodes_Left.d: A brachial lymph nodes (or lateral group) are group of four to six lymph nodes which lies in relation to the medial and posterior aspects of the axillary vein; the afferents of these glands drain the whole arm with the exception of that portion whose vessels accompany the cephalic vein. The efferent vessels pass partly to the central and subclavicular groups of axillary glands and partly to the inferior deep cervical glands.

Lymph_Lateral_Axillary_Nodes_Right.d: A brachial lymph nodes (or lateral group) are group of four to six lymph nodes which lies in relation to the medial and posterior aspects of the axillary vein; the afferents of these glands drain the whole arm with the exception of that portion whose vessels accompany the cephalic vein. The efferent vessels pass partly to the central and subclavicular groups of axillary glands and partly to the inferior deep cervical glands.

Lymph_Lateral_Caval_Nodes.d: The lateral caval nodes are located on the right of the inferior vena cava.

Lymph_Lateral_Common_Iliac_Nodes.d: Those of the common iliac nodes located on the lateral side of the vascular axis.

Lymph_Lateral_Sacral_Nodes_Left.d: They are located against the sacrum; for the prostate and the neck of uterus.

Lymph_Lateral_Sacral_Nodes_Right.d: They are located against the sacrum; for the prostate and the neck of uterus.

Lymph_Left_Colic_Nodes.d: The left colic nodes follow the path of the left colic artery. The middle colic nodes follow the path of the middle colic artery. The right colic nodes follow the path of the right colic artery.

Lymph_Mandibular_Node_Left.d: the mandibular node is located on the external side of the mandible.

Lymph_Mandibular_Node_Right.d: the mandibular node is located on the external side of the mandible.

Lymph_Mastoid_Nodes_Left.d: The mastoid lymph nodes (retroauricular lymph nodes or posterior auricular glands) are a small group of lymph nodes, usually two in number, located just beneath the ear, on the mastoid insertion of the sternocleidomastoideus muscle, beneath the posterior auricular muscle. Their mastoid lymph nodes receives lymph from the posterior part of the temporoparietal region, the upper part of the cranial surface of the visible ear and the back of the ear canal. The lymph then passes to the superior deep cervical glands.

Lymph_Mastoid_Nodes_Right.d: The mastoid lymph nodes (retroauricular lymph nodes or posterior auricular glands) are a small group of lymph nodes, usually two in number, located just beneath the ear, on the mastoid insertion of the sternocleidomastoideus muscle, beneath the posterior auricular muscle. Their mastoid lymph nodes receives lymph from the posterior part of the temporoparietal region, the upper part of the cranial surface of the visible ear and the back of the ear canal. The lymph then passes to the superior deep cervical glands.

Lymph_Medial_Common_Iliac_Nodes.d: Those of the common iliac nodes located on the medial side of the vascular axis.

Lymph_Middle_Colic_Nodes.d: The left colic nodes follow the path of the left colic artery. The middle colic nodes follow the path of the middle colic artery. The right colic nodes follow the path of the right colic artery.

Lymph_Nasolabial_Node_Left.d: The nasolabial lymph node is a facial node found near the nose and upper lip.

Lymph_Nasolabial_Node_Right.d: The nasolabial lymph node is a facial node found near the nose and upper lip.

Lymph_Node_Of_Arch_Of_Azygos_Vein.n: Node of arch of azygos vein

Lymph_Occipital_Nodes_Left.d: The occipital lymph nodes, one to three in number, are located on the back of the head close to the margin of the trapezius and resting on the insertion of the semispinalis capitis. Their afferent vessels drain the occipital region of the scalp, while their efferents pass to the superior deep cervical glands.

Lymph_Occipital_Nodes_Right.d: The occipital lymph nodes, one to three in number, are located on the back of the head close to the margin of the trapezius and resting on the insertion of the semispinalis capitis. Their afferent vessels drain the occipital region of the scalp, while their efferents pass to the superior deep cervical glands.

Lymph_Palatine_Tonsil_Left.d: Palatine tonsils, commonly called the tonsils and occasionally called the faucial tonsils, are tonsils located on the left and right sides at the back of the throat, which can often be seen as flesh-colored, pinkish lumps. Tonsils only present as "white lumps" if they are inflamed or infected with symptoms of exudates (pus drainage) and severe swelling. Tonsillitis is an inflammation of the tonsils and will often, but not necessarily, cause a sore throat and fever. In chronic cases tonsillectomy may be indicated.

Lymph_Palatine_Tonsil_Right.d: Palatine tonsils, commonly called the tonsils and occasionally called the faucial tonsils, are tonsils located on the left and right sides at the back of the throat, which can often be seen as flesh-colored, pinkish lumps. Tonsils only present as "white lumps" if they are inflamed or infected with symptoms of exudates (pus drainage) and severe swelling. Tonsillitis is an inflammation of the tonsils and will often, but not necessarily, cause a sore throat and fever. In chronic cases tonsillectomy may be indicated.

Lymph_Paracolic_Superior_Mesenteric_Node.d: Those of the superior mesenteric nodes located next to the colon.

Lymph_Parasternal_Nodes_Left.d: The parasternal lymph nodes (or sternal glands) are placed at the anterior ends of the intercostal spaces, by the side of the internal thoracic artery. They derive afferents from the mamma; from the deeper structures of the anterior abdominal wall above the level of the umbilicus; from the upper surface of the liver through a small group of glands which lie behind the xiphoid process; and from the deeper parts of the anterior portion of the thoracic wall. Their efferents usually unite to form a single trunk on either side; this may open directly into the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins, or that of the right side may join the right subclavian trunk, and that of the left...

Lymph_Parasternal_Nodes_Right.d: The parasternal lymph nodes (or sternal glands) are placed at the anterior ends of the intercostal spaces, by the side of the internal thoracic artery. They derive afferents from the mamma; from the deeper structures of the anterior abdominal wall above the level of the umbilicus; from the upper surface of the liver through a small group of glands which lie behind the xiphoid process; and from the deeper parts of the anterior portion of the thoracic wall. Their efferents usually unite to form a single trunk on either side; this may open directly into the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins, or that of the right side may join the right subclavian trunk, and that of the left...

Lymph_Paratracheal_Cervical_Nodes.d: The right and left paratracheal nodes (or paratracheal chains) are groups of lymph nodes located laterally to the trachea; unlike the pretracheal nodes that are located in front of it.

Lymph_Posterior_Axillary_Nodes_Left.d: A posterior or subscapular group of six or seven glands is placed along the lower margin of the posterior wall of the axilla in the course of the subscapular artery. The afferents of this group drain the skin and muscles of the lower part of the back of the neck and of the posterior thoracic wall; their efferents pass to the central group of axillary glands.

Lymph_Posterior_Axillary_Nodes_Right.d: A posterior or subscapular group of six or seven glands is placed along the lower margin of the posterior wall of the axilla in the course of the subscapular artery. The afferents of this group drain the skin and muscles of the lower part of the back of the neck and of the posterior thoracic wall; their efferents pass to the central group of axillary glands.

Lymph_Postvesical_Nodes.d: Those of the paravesical nodes located behind the urinary bladder.

Lymph_Pre_Aortic_Nodes.d: The preaortic lymph nodes lie in front of the aorta, and may be divided into celiac lymph nodes, superior mesenteric lymph nodes, and inferior mesenteric lymph nodes groups, arranged around the origins of the corresponding arteries. The celiac lymph nodes are grouped into three sets: the gastric, hepatic and splenic lymph nodes. These groups also form their own subgroups. The superior mesenteric lymph nodes are grouped into three sets: the mesenteric, ileocolic and mesocolic lymph nodes. The inferior mesenteric lymph nodes have a subgroup of pararectal lymph nodes. The preaortic lymph nodes receive a few vessels from the lateral aortic lymph nodes, but their principal afferents are derived...

Lymph_Precaecal_Nodes.d: The precaecal nodes are located along the anterior caecal artery.

Lymph_Precaval_Nodes.d: They are located in front of the inferior vena cava.

Lymph_Prepericardial_Nodes.d: Located between the sternum and the pericardium, the prepericardial nodes drain the sternum and the anterior part of the pericardium. Evacuation: Parasternal nodes

Lymph_Pretracheal_Nodes_Left.d: The pretracheal lymph nodes are lymph nodes located anterior to the trachea in the neck.

Lymph_Pretracheal_Nodes_Right.d: The pretracheal lymph nodes are lymph nodes located anterior to the trachea in the neck.

Lymph_Prevertebral_Nodes.d: The prevertebral lymph nodes are located between the oesophagus and the vertebral column.

Lymph_Prevesical_Nodes.d: Those of the vesical nodes located between the urinary bladder and the pubic symphysis.

Lymph_Retro_Aortic_Nodes.d: The retroaortic lymph nodes (or postaortic lymph nodes) are placed below the cisterna chyli, on the bodies of the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae. They receive lymphatic trunks from the lateral and preaortic glands, while their efferents end in the cisterna chyli.

Lymph_Retrocaecal_Nodes.d: The retrocaecal are located along the posterior caecal artery.

Lymph_Retrocaval_Nodes.d: The retrocaval nodes are located behind the inferior vena cava.

Lymph_Retropharyngeal_Nodes_Left.d: The retropharyngeal lymph nodes, from one to three in number, lie in the buccopharyngeal fascia, behind the upper part of the pharynx and in front of the arch of the atlas, being separated, however, from the latter by the Longus capitis. Their afferents drain the nasal cavities, the nasal part of the pharynx, and the auditory tubes. Their efferents pass to the superior deep cervical lymph nodes. They are in the retropharyngeal space. They frequently disappear by age 4-5. (This is why retropharyngeal abscess is rare in older children.)

Lymph_Retropharyngeal_Nodes_Right.d: The retropharyngeal lymph nodes, from one to three in number, lie in the buccopharyngeal fascia, behind the upper part of the pharynx and in front of the arch of the atlas, being separated, however, from the latter by the Longus capitis. Their afferents drain the nasal cavities, the nasal part of the pharynx, and the auditory tubes. Their efferents pass to the superior deep cervical lymph nodes. They are in the retropharyngeal space. They frequently disappear by age 4-5. (This is why retropharyngeal abscess is rare in older children.)

Lymph_Retropyloric_Nodes.d: On the dorsal side of the pyloric part of the stomach.

Lymph_Right_Colic_Nodes.d: The left colic nodes follow the path of the left colic artery. The middle colic nodes follow the path of the middle colic artery. The right colic nodes follow the path of the right colic artery.

Lymph_Right_Gastric_Nodes.d: On the lesser curvature of stomach, they follow the path of the left/right gastric arteries. they drain the stomach and evacuate in the coeliac nodes.

Lymph_Right_Gastro_Omental_Nodes.d: The right and left gastro-omental nodes are located on the great curvature of stomach on the path of the left/right gastro-omental arteries. They drain the stomach and the greater omentum, on the right towards the hepatic nodes, and on the left to the splenic nodes and pancreatic nodes.

Lymph_Sigmoid_Nodes.d: Located along the sigmoid artery, for the sigmoid colon and the contiguous colic segment.

Lymph_Splenic_Nodes.d: The splenic lymph nodes are found at the splenic hilum and in relation to the tail of the pancreas (pancreaticolienal lymph nodes). Their afferents are derived from the stomach, spleen, and pancreas. The splenic lymph nodes empty into the suprapancreatic, infrapancreatic and omental lymph nodes, which then drain to the coeliac nodes and cisterna chyli.

Lymph_Subaortic_Nodes.d: Those of the common iliac nodes located beneath the aortic bifurcation, in front of the 4th lumbar vertebra (Vertebra T4).

Lymph_Submandibular_Nodes_Left.d: The submandibular lymph nodes (submaxillary glands in older texts), three to six in number, are lymph nodes beneath the body of the mandible in the submandibular triangle, and rest on the superficial surface of the submandibular gland. One gland, the middle gland of Stahr, which lies on the facial artery as it turns over the mandible, is the most constant of the series; small lymph glands are sometimes found on the deep surface of the submandibular gland. The afferents of the submandibular glands drain the medial canthus, the cheek, the side of the nose, the upper lip, the lateral part of the lower lip, the gums, and the anterior part of the margin of the tongue. Efferent lymph vessels from...

Lymph_Submandibular_Nodes_Right.d: The submandibular lymph nodes (submaxillary glands in older texts), three to six in number, are lymph nodes beneath the body of the mandible in the submandibular triangle, and rest on the superficial surface of the submandibular gland. One gland, the middle gland of Stahr, which lies on the facial artery as it turns over the mandible, is the most constant of the series; small lymph glands are sometimes found on the deep surface of the submandibular gland. The afferents of the submandibular glands drain the medial canthus, the cheek, the side of the nose, the upper lip, the lateral part of the lower lip, the gums, and the anterior part of the margin of the tongue. Efferent lymph vessels from...

Lymph_Submental_Nodes_Left.d: The submental glands (or suprahyoid) are situated between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscle and the hyoid bone. Their afferents drain the central portions of the lower lip and floor of the mouth and the apex of the tongue. Their efferents pass partly to the submandibular lymph nodes and partly to a gland of the deep cervical group situated on the internal jugular vein at the level of the cricoid cartilage.

Lymph_Submental_Nodes_Right.d: The submental glands (or suprahyoid) are situated between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscle and the hyoid bone. Their afferents drain the central portions of the lower lip and floor of the mouth and the apex of the tongue. Their efferents pass partly to the submandibular lymph nodes and partly to a gland of the deep cervical group situated on the internal jugular vein at the level of the cricoid cartilage.

Lymph_Subpyloric_Nodes.d: On the caudal side of the pyloric part of the stomach.

Lymph_Superficial_Popliteal_Nodes_Left.d: The superficial popliteal nodes are located at the proximal extremity of the lesser saphenous vein and drain the lymph of the lateral border of the foot and of the leg. Evacuation: frontwards through the adductor hiatus of the adductor magnus, in the deep inguinal nodes.

Lymph_Superficial_Popliteal_Nodes_Right.d: The superficial popliteal nodes are located at the proximal extremity of the lesser saphenous vein and drain the lymph of the lateral border of the foot and of the leg. Evacuation: frontwards through the adductor hiatus of the adductor magnus, in the deep inguinal nodes.

Lymph_Superior_Diaphragmatic_Nodes.d: The superior diaphragmatic lymph nodes lie on the thoracic aspect of the diaphragm, and consist of three sets – anterior, middle, and posterior. The anterior set comprises (a) two or three small nodes behind the base of the xiphoid process, which receive afferents from the convex surface of the liver, and (b) one or two nodes on either side near the junction of the seventh rib with its cartilage, which receive lymphatic vessels from the front part of the diaphragm. The efferent vessels of the anterior set pass to the parasternal lymph nodes. The middle set consists of two or three nodes on either side close to where the phrenic nerves enter the diaphragm. On the right side some of the lymph...

Lymph_Superior_Gluteal_Nodes_Left.d: Located along the superior gluteal artery for the wall of the pelvis.

Lymph_Superior_Gluteal_Nodes_Right.d: Located along the superior gluteal artery for the wall of the pelvis.

Lymph_Superior_Pancreatic_Nodes.d: On the superior border of pancreas.

Lymph_Superior_Pancreaticoduodenal_Nodes.d: Superior part of the pancreaticoduodenal nodes. They evacuate in the hepatic nodes.

Lymph_Supraclavicular_Nodes_Left.d: Supraclavicular lymph nodes are lymph nodes found above the clavicle, that can be felt in the supraclavicular fossa. The supraclavicular lymph nodes on the left side are called Virchow's nodes. It leads to an appreciable mass that can be recognized clinically, called Troisier sign.

Lymph_Supraclavicular_Nodes_Right.d: Supraclavicular lymph nodes are lymph nodes found above the clavicle, that can be felt in the supraclavicular fossa. The supraclavicular lymph nodes on the left side are called Virchow's nodes. It leads to an appreciable mass that can be recognized clinically, called Troisier sign.

Lymph_Suprapyloric_Node.d: Above the pyloric part of stomach.

Lymph_Supratrochlear_Nodes_Left.d: One or two supratrochlear lymph nodes are placed above the medial epicondyle of the humerus, medial to the basilic vein. Their afferents drain the middle, ring, and little fingers, the medial portion of the hand, and the superficial area over the ulnar side of the forearm; these vessels are, however, in free communication with the other lymphatic vessels of the forearm. Their efferents accompany the basilic vein and join the deeper vessels. They are distinguished in Terminologia anatomica from the "epitrochlear" (or "cubital") lymph nodes, but the region is similar.

Lymph_Supratrochlear_Nodes_Right.d: One or two supratrochlear lymph nodes are placed above the medial epicondyle of the humerus, medial to the basilic vein. Their afferents drain the middle, ring, and little fingers, the medial portion of the hand, and the superficial area over the ulnar side of the forearm; these vessels are, however, in free communication with the other lymphatic vessels of the forearm. Their efferents accompany the basilic vein and join the deeper vessels. They are distinguished in Terminologia anatomica from the "epitrochlear" (or "cubital") lymph nodes, but the region is similar.

Lymph_Thyroid_Nodes_Left.d: The thyroid lymph nodes are deep anterior cervical lymph nodes found near the thyroid gland on the neck.

Lymph_Thyroid_Nodes_Right.d: The thyroid lymph nodes are deep anterior cervical lymph nodes found near the thyroid gland on the neck.

Muscle_Abdominal_Part_Of_Pectoralis_Majo.n: Abdominal part of pectoralis major muscle
Muscle_Abdominal_Part_Of_Pectoralis_Majo.d: The more frequent variations include greater or less extent of attachment to the ribs and sternum, varying size of the abdominal part or its absence, greater or less extent of separation of sternocostal and clavicular parts, fusion of clavicular part with deltoid, and decussation in front of the sternum.

Muscle_Abdominal_Part_Of_Pectoralis_Majo.n: Abdominal part of pectoralis major muscle
Muscle_Abdominal_Part_Of_Pectoralis_Majo.d: The more frequent variations include greater or less extent of attachment to the ribs and sternum, varying size of the abdominal part or its absence, greater or less extent of separation of sternocostal and clavicular parts, fusion of clavicular part with deltoid, and decussation in front of the sternum.

Muscle_Abductor_Digiti_Minimi_Of_Foot_Le.d: The abductor digiti minimi (abductor minimi digiti, abductor digiti quinti) is a muscle which lies along the lateral (outer) border of the foot, and is in relation by its medial margin with the lateral plantar artery, vein and nerves. Its homolog in the arm is the abductor digiti minimi muscle in the hand.

Muscle_Abductor_Digiti_Minimi_Of_Foot_Ri.d: The abductor digiti minimi (abductor minimi digiti, abductor digiti quinti) is a muscle which lies along the lateral (outer) border of the foot, and is in relation by its medial margin with the lateral plantar artery, vein and nerves. Its homolog in the arm is the abductor digiti minimi muscle in the hand.

Muscle_Abductor_Digiti_Minimi_Of_Hand_Le.d: In human anatomy, the abductor digiti minimi (abductor minimi digiti, abductor digiti quinti, ADM) is a skeletal muscle situated on the ulnar border of the palm of the hand. It forms the ulnar border of the palm and its spindle-like shape defines the hypothenar eminence of the palm together with the skin, connective tissue, and fat surrounding it. Its main function is to pull the little finger away from the other fingers (i.e. abduction).

Muscle_Abductor_Digiti_Minimi_Of_Hand_Ri.d: In human anatomy, the abductor digiti minimi (abductor minimi digiti, abductor digiti quinti, ADM) is a skeletal muscle situated on the ulnar border of the palm of the hand. Muscle_Abductor_Hallucis_Left.d: The abductor hallucis muscle is an intrinsic muscle of the foot. It participates in the abduction and flexion of the great toe.

Muscle_Abductor_Hallucis_Right.d: The abductor hallucis muscle is an intrinsic muscle of the foot. It participates in the abduction and flexion of the great toe.

Muscle_Abductor_Pollicis_Brevis_Left.d: The abductor pollicis brevis is a muscle in the hand that functions as an abductor of the thumb.

Muscle_Abductor_Pollicis_Brevis_Right.d: The abductor pollicis brevis is a muscle in the hand that functions as an abductor of the thumb.

Muscle_Abductor_Pollicis_Longus_Left.d: In human anatomy, the abductor pollicis longus (APL) is one of the extrinsic muscles of the hand. Its major function is to abduct the thumb at the wrist. Its tendon forms the anterior border of the anatomical snuffbox.

Muscle_Abductor_Pollicis_Longus_Right.d: In human anatomy, the abductor pollicis longus (APL) is one of the extrinsic muscles of the hand. Its major function is to abduct the thumb at the wrist. Its tendon forms the anterior border of the anatomical snuffbox.

Muscle_Acromial_Part_Of_Deltoid_Left.d: The deltoid muscle is the muscle forming the rounded contour of the human shoulder. It is also known as the 'common shoulder muscle', particularly in other animals such as the domestic cat. Anatomically, the deltoid muscle appears to be made up of three distinct sets of muscle fibers, namely the -anterior or clavicular part (pars clavicularis) -posterior or scapular part (pars scapularis) -intermediate or acromial part (pars acromialis) However, electromyography suggests that it consists of at least seven groups that can be independently coordinated by the nervous system. It was previously called the deltoideus (plural deltoidei) and the name is still used by some anatomists. It is called...

Muscle_Adductor_Brevis_Left.d: The adductor brevis is a muscle in the thigh situated immediately deep to the pectineus and adductor longus. It belongs to the adductor muscle group. The main function of the adductor brevis is to pull the thigh medially. The adductor brevis and the rest of the adductor muscle group is also used to stabilize left to right movements of the trunk, when standing on both feet, or to balance when standing on a moving surface. The adductor muscle group is used pressing the thighs together to ride a horse, and kicking with the inside of the foot in soccer or swimming. Last, they contribute to flexion of the thigh when running or against resistance (squats, jumping, etc.).

Muscle_Adductor_Brevis_Right.d: The adductor brevis is a muscle in the thigh situated immediately deep to the pectineus and adductor longus. It belongs to the adductor muscle group. The main function of the adductor brevis is to pull the thigh medially. The adductor brevis and the rest of the adductor muscle group is also used to stabilize left to right movements of the trunk, when standing on both feet, or to balance when standing on a moving surface. The adductor muscle group is used pressing the thighs together to ride a horse, and kicking with the inside of the foot in soccer or swimming. Last, they contribute to flexion of the thigh when running or against resistance (squats, jumping, etc.).

Muscle_Adductor_Longus_Left.d: In the human body, the adductor longus is a skeletal muscle located in the thigh. One of the adductor muscles of the hip, its main function is to adduct the thigh and it is innervated by the obturator nerve. It forms the medial wall of the femoral triangle.

Muscle_Adductor_Longus_Right.d: In the human body, the adductor longus is a skeletal muscle located in the thigh. One of the adductor muscles of the hip, its main function is to adduct the thigh and it is innervated by the obturator nerve. It forms the medial wall of the femoral triangle.

Muscle_Adductor_Magnus_Left.d: The adductor magnus is a large triangular muscle, situated on the medial side of the thigh. It consists of two parts. The portion which arises from the ischiopubic ramus (a small part of the inferior ramus of the pubis, and the inferior ramus of the ischium) is called the pubofemoral portion, adductor portion, or adductor minimus, and the portion arising from the tuberosity of the ischium is called the ischiocondylar portion, extensor portion, or "hamstring portion". Due to its common embryonic origin, innervation, and action the ischiocondylar portion (or hamstring portion) is often considered part of the hamstring group of muscles. The ischiocondylar portion of the adductor magnus is...

Muscle_Adductor_Magnus_Right.d: The adductor magnus is a large triangular muscle, situated on the medial side of the thigh. It consists of two parts. The portion which arises from the ischiopubic ramus (a small part of the inferior ramus of the pubis, and the inferior ramus of the ischium) is called the pubofemoral portion, adductor portion, or adductor minimus, and the portion arising from the tuberosity of the ischium is called the ischiocondylar portion, extensor portion, or "hamstring portion". Muscle_Adductor_Minimus_Left.d: Small and flat skeletal muscle in the thigh which constitutes the upper, lateral part of the adductor magnus muscle. It adducts and laterally rotates the femur. The adductor minimus originates on the pelvis at the inferior ramus of the pubis as the anterior-most part of the adductor magnus. It is inserted on the back of the femur at the medial lip of the linea aspera and thus crosses the proximal part of the true adductor magnus.

Muscle_Adductor_Minimus_Right.d: Small and flat skeletal muscle in the thigh which constitutes the upper, lateral part of the adductor magnus muscle. It adducts and laterally rotates the femur. The adductor minimus originates on the pelvis at the inferior ramus of the pubis as the anterior-most part of the adductor magnus. It is inserted on the back of the femur at the medial lip of the linea aspera and thus crosses the proximal part of the true adductor magnus.

Muscle_Anconeus_Left.d: The anconeus muscle (or anconaeus/anconæus) is a small muscle on the posterior aspect of the elbow joint. Some consider anconeus to be a continuation of the triceps brachii muscle. Some sources consider it to be part of the posterior compartment of the arm, while others consider it part of the posterior compartment of the forearm.The anconeus muscle can easily be palpated just lateral to the olecranon process of the ulna.

Muscle_Anconeus_Right.d: The anconeus muscle (or anconaeus/anconæus) is a small muscle on the posterior aspect of the elbow joint. Some consider anconeus to be a continuation of the triceps brachii muscle. Some sources consider it to be part of the posterior compartment of the arm, while others consider it part of the posterior compartment of the forearm.The anconeus muscle can easily be palpated just lateral to the olecranon process of the ulna.

Muscle_Anterior_Belly_Of_Digastric_Left.d: The digastric muscle (also digastricus) (named digastric as it has two 'bellies') is a small muscle located under the jaw. The term "digastric muscle" refers to this specific muscle. However, other muscles that have two separate muscle bellies include the suspensory muscle of duodenum, omohyoid, occipitofrontalis. It lies below the body of the mandible, and extends, in a curved form, from the mastoid notch to the mandibular symphysis. It belongs to the suprahyoid muscles group. A broad aponeurotic layer is given off from the tendon of the digastric muscle on either side, to be attached to the body and greater cornu of the hyoid bone; this is termed the suprahyoid aponeurosis.

Muscle_Anterior_Belly_Of_Digastric_Right.d: The digastric muscle (also digastricus) (named digastric as it has two 'bellies') is a small muscle located under the jaw. Muscle_Ary_Epiglottic_Part_Of_Oblique_Ar.n: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle
Muscle_Ary_Epiglottic_Part_Of_Oblique_Ar.d: Origin apex of arytenoid cartilage. Insertion: border of epiglottis. Support of the ary-epiglottic fold. Lower the epiglottis.

Muscle_Ary_Epiglottic_Part_Of_Oblique_Ar.n: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle
Muscle_Ary_Epiglottic_Part_Of_Oblique_Ar.d: Origin apex of arytenoid cartilage. Insertion: border of epiglottis. Support of the ary-epiglottic fold. Lower the epiglottis.

Muscle_Ascending_Part_Of_Trapezius_Left.d: The trapezius is a large paired trapezoid-shaped surface muscle that extends longitudinally from the occipital bone to the lower thoracic vertebrae of the spine and laterally to the spine of the scapula. It moves the scapula and supports the arm. The trapezius has three functional parts: an upper (descending) part which supports the weight of the arm; a middle region (transverse), which retracts the scapula; and a lower (ascending) part which medially rotates and depresses the scapula.

Muscle_Ascending_Part_Of_Trapezius_Right.d: The trapezius is a large paired trapezoid-shaped surface muscle that extends longitudinally from the occipital bone to the lower thoracic vertebrae of the spine and laterally to the spine of the scapula. The trapezius has three functional parts: an upper (descending) part which supports the weight of the arm; a middle region (transverse), which retracts the scapula; and a lower (ascending) part which medially rotates and depresses the scapula.

Muscle_Brachialis_Left.d: The brachialis (brachialis anticus) Also known as the Teichmann muscle, is a muscle in the upper arm that flexes the elbow. It lies deeper than the biceps brachii, and makes up part of the floor of the region known as the cubital fossa (elbow pit). The brachialis is the prime mover of elbow flexion generating about 50% more power than the biceps.

Muscle_Brachialis_Right.d: The brachialis (brachialis anticus) Also known as the Teichmann muscle, is a muscle in the upper arm that flexes the elbow. It lies deeper than the biceps brachii, and makes up part of the floor of the region known as the cubital fossa (elbow pit). The brachialis is the prime mover of elbow flexion generating about 50% more power than the biceps.

Muscle_Brachioradialis_Left.d: The brachioradialis is a muscle of the forearm that flexes the forearm at the elbow. It is also capable of both pronation and supination, depending on the position of the forearm. It is attached to the distal styloid process of the radius by way of the brachioradialis tendon, and to the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.

Muscle_Brachioradialis_Right.d: The brachioradialis is a muscle of the forearm that flexes the forearm at the elbow. It is also capable of both pronation and supination, depending on the position of the forearm. It is attached to the distal styloid process of the radius by way of the brachioradialis tendon, and to the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.

Muscle_Bucinator_Left.d: The bucinator is a thin quadrilateral muscle occupying the interval between the maxilla and the mandible at the side of the face. It forms the anterior part of the cheek or the lateral wall of the oral cavity.

Muscle_Bucinator_Right.d: The bucinator is a thin quadrilateral muscle occupying the interval between the maxilla and the mandible at the side of the face. It forms the anterior part of the cheek or the lateral wall of the oral cavity.

Muscle_Calcaneal_Tendon_Left.d: The calcaneal tendon or heel cord, also known as the Achilles tendon, is a tendon at the back of the lower leg, and is the thickest in the human body. It serves to attach the plantaris, gastrocnemius (calf) and soleus muscles to the calcaneus (heel) bone. These muscles, acting via the tendon, cause plantar flexion of the foot at the ankle joint, and (except the soleus) flexion at the knee. Abnormalities of the calcaneal tendon include inflammation (calcaneal tendinitis), degeneration, rupture, and becoming embedded with cholesterol deposits (xanthomas). The calcaneal tendon was named in 1693 after the Greek hero calcaneal.

Muscle_Calcaneal_Tendon_Right.d: The calcaneal tendon or heel cord, also known as the Achilles tendon, is a tendon at the back of the lower leg, and is the thickest in the human body. Muscle_Clavicular_Head_Of_Pectoralis_Maj.n: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Muscle_Clavicular_Head_Of_Pectoralis_Maj.d: The pectoralis major (from Latin pectus 'breast') is a thick, fan-shaped or triangular convergent muscle, situated at the chest of the human body. It makes up the bulk of the chest muscles and lies under the breast. Beneath the pectoralis major is the pectoralis minor, a thin, triangular muscle. The pectoralis major's primary functions are flexion, adduction, and internal rotation of the humerus. The pectoral major may colloquially be referred to as "pecs", "pectoral muscle" or "chest muscle" due to it being the largest and most superficial muscle in the chest area.

Muscle_Clavicular_Head_Of_Pectoralis_Maj.n: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Muscle_Coccygeus_Left.d: The coccygeus muscle or ischiococcygeus is a muscle of the pelvic floor, located posterior to levator ani and anterior to the sacrospinous ligament.

Muscle_Coccygeus_Right.d: The coccygeus muscle or ischiococcygeus is a muscle of the pelvic floor, located posterior to levator ani and anterior to the sacrospinous ligament.

Muscle_Coracobrachialis_Left.d: The coracobrachialis muscle is the smallest of the three muscles that attach to the coracoid process of the scapula. (The other two muscles are pectoralis minor and the short head of the biceps brachii.) It is situated at the upper and medial part of the arm.

Muscle_Coracobrachialis_Right.d: The coracobrachialis muscle is the smallest of the three muscles that attach to the coracoid process of the scapula. (The other two muscles are pectoralis minor and the short head of the biceps brachii.) It is situated at the upper and medial part of the arm.

Muscle_Corrugator_Supercilii_Left.d: The corrugator supercilii muscle is a small, narrow, pyramidal muscle close to the eye. It arises from the medial end of the superciliary arch, and inserts into the deep surface of the skin of the eyebrow. It draws the eyebrow downward and medially, producing the vertical wrinkles of the forehead.

Muscle_Corrugator_Supercilii_Right.d: The corrugator supercilii muscle is a small, narrow, pyramidal muscle close to the eye. Muscle_Deep_Head_Of_Flexor_Pollicis_Brev.n: Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Muscle_Deep_Head_Of_Flexor_Pollicis_Brev.d: The flexor pollicis brevis is a muscle in the hand that flexes the thumb. It is one of three thenar muscles. It has both a superficial part and a deep part.

Muscle_Deep_Head_Of_Flexor_Pollicis_Brev.n: Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Muscle_Deep_Head_Of_Flexor_Pollicis_Brev.d: The flexor pollicis brevis is a muscle in the hand that flexes the thumb. It is one of three thenar muscles. It has both a superficial part and a deep part.

Muscle_Deep_Head_Of_Pronator_Teres_Left.d: The deep head (or ulnar head) of pronator teres is a thin fasciculus, which arises from the medial side of the coronoid process of the ulna, and joins the superficial head at an acute angle.

Muscle_Deep_Head_Of_Pronator_Teres_Right.d: The deep head (or ulnar head) of pronator teres is a thin fasciculus, which arises from the medial side of the coronoid process of the ulna, and joins the superficial head at an acute angle.

Muscle_Deep_Part_Of_Masseter_Left.d: In human anatomy, the masseter is one of the muscles of mastication. Found only in mammals, it is particularly powerful in herbivores to facilitate chewing of plant matter. The most obvious muscle of mastication is the masseter muscle, since it is the most superficial and one of the strongest.

Muscle_Deep_Part_Of_Masseter_Right.d: In human anatomy, the masseter is one of the muscles of mastication. Found only in mammals, it is particularly powerful in herbivores to facilitate chewing of plant matter. The most obvious muscle of mastication is the masseter muscle, since it is the most superficial and one of the strongest.

Muscle_Depressor_Anguli_Oris_Left.d: The depressor anguli oris muscle (triangularis muscle) is a facial muscle. It originates from the mandible and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It is associated with frowning, as it depresses the corner of the mouth.

Muscle_Depressor_Anguli_Oris_Right.d: The depressor anguli oris muscle (triangularis muscle) is a facial muscle. It originates from the mandible and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It is associated with frowning, as it depresses the corner of the mouth.

Muscle_Depressor_Labii_Inferioris_Left.d: The depressor labii inferioris (or quadratus labii inferioris) is a facial muscle. It helps to lower the bottom lip.

Muscle_Depressor_Labii_Inferioris_Right.d: The depressor labii inferioris (or quadratus labii inferioris) is a facial muscle. It helps to lower the bottom lip.

Muscle_Depressor_Septi_Nasi_Left.d: The depressor septi nasi muscle (or depressor alae nasi muscle) is a muscle of the face. It connects the incisive fossa of the maxilla and the orbicularis oris muscle to the nasal septum of the nose. It draws the ala of the nose downwards, reducing the size of the nostrils.

Muscle_Depressor_Septi_Nasi_Right.d: The depressor septi nasi muscle (or depressor alae nasi muscle) is a muscle of the face. It connects the incisive fossa of the maxilla and the orbicularis oris muscle to the nasal septum of the nose. It draws the ala of the nose downwards, reducing the size of the nostrils.
